articles.title: New Endangered Wildlife Mural Unveiled in Middleton
articles.excerpt: A 15-metre-high wildlife mural has been unveiled on Oldham Road in Middleton, created through an international arts exchange project focusing on endangered species and ecosystems.
articles.content_html:
A new 15-metre-high wildlife mural has been unveiled on Oldham Road in Middleton town centre, created as part of an international arts exchange project between artists from Rochdale and Kenya. The mural, which features various endangered species, is part of the Endangered Exchange initiative led by Rochdale artist Hayley Garner, also known as AYLO, and Victoria Firth, founder of The Wild Mural Project.

The artwork, measuring approximately 15 metres high and 10 metres wide, showcases a hen harrier, large heath butterfly, emperor dragonfly, sphagnum moss, and wildfires. It also includes the phrase "Save our tomorrow today" in Swahili, alongside design elements inspired by Kanga fabric, which is significant in Kenyan culture. The project has been developed in partnership with the Lancashire Wildlife Trust.

Ninah Tanya, a Kenyan artist who participated in the project, expressed her enthusiasm about the mural, stating, "This is the biggest mural I've worked on and it has been a wonderful experience." She spent two weeks in Middleton as part of her residency, having been mentored by Victoria Firth in Kenya over the past year. Local artist Jamie Buckley is set to travel to Kenya next month to continue the exchange, where he will engage with local communities and work on a second mural.

Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council, highlighted the mural's significance in raising awareness about climate change and its impact on wildlife. The project is part of the Rochdale Creates cultural programme and is supported by various local organisations, including The Butterfly Effected CIC and Rochdale Development Agency. A documentary is being produced to capture the artists' journeys and the cultural exchange.

articles.title: Middleton's Regeneration Efforts Advance with Key Announcements
articles.excerpt: Middleton's regeneration initiative has gained momentum with three significant announcements, including plans for the historic Middleton Old Grammar School and the repurposing of the Scout Hut for community use.
articles.content_html:
Middleton's regeneration initiative has taken a significant step forward with three key announcements made during an event at Middleton Arena on 16 September 2026. The event, which attracted over 500 residents and local business leaders, aimed to update the community on the progress of the Mayoral Development Corporation and the results of the engagement exercise titled 'Our Town, Our Future'.

One of the major announcements was regarding the historic Middleton Old Grammar School, located on Boarshaw Road. Recently acquired by Rochdale Borough Council, the building is expected to announce a new tenant by the end of the year. Originally founded in 1582 to provide free education, the school has served various purposes over the years, including as a wedding and events venue. The council plans to conduct a feasibility study to explore options for repairing, refurbishing, and reopening the building for community use.

Additionally, the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill and the adjacent London House, a 1960s office block. The aim is to bring Warwick Mill back into use, potentially as new housing, while London House is set to be demolished. These developments are part of a broader strategy to rejuvenate the area and enhance local amenities.

In another positive development, the Middleton Scout Hut on Long Street, which has been vacant for 13 years, will be repurposed as a community venue. The council has agreed to a long-term lease with the Groundwork Trust, a charitable organisation. Plans for the Scout Hut include creating a hub for workshops focused on ecology and construction skills, as well as providing a space for local environmental projects and community group activities.

articles.title: Businessman Pleads Guilty to Selling £2.4 Million Worth of Fake Clothes in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: A businessman from Hale Barns has pleaded guilty to possession of counterfeit goods with intent to supply after a haul of fake designer clothing worth £2.4 million was discovered in Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

Live updates, newest first.

21:14, 16 September 2026

A businessman from Hale Barns has pleaded guilty to possession of counterfeit goods after over £2.4 million in fake designer clothing was discovered at a Rochdale business.

19:06, 16 September 2026

A businessman from Hale Barns has pleaded guilty to possession of counterfeit goods with intent to supply after a haul of fake designer clothing worth £2.4 million was discovered in Rochdale.

19:06, 16 September 2026

A businessman from Hale Barns has pleaded guilty to possession of counterfeit goods with intent to supply after a haul of fake designer clothing was discovered in Rochdale, valued at £2.4 million.

18:47, 16 September 2026

Assum Malik from Hale Barns has pleaded guilty to possession of counterfeit goods with intent to supply after a haul of fake merchandise was discovered in Rochdale.

A businessman from Hale Barns has pleaded guilty to possession of counterfeit goods with intent to supply after a haul of fake designer clothing worth £2.4 million was uncovered at a business in Rochdale on January 28, 2022. Assum Malik, of High Elm Road, initially entered a not guilty plea but changed his plea during a hearing at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court on September 14, 2026.

During the court proceedings, Malik disputed the total value of the counterfeit goods, claiming it was closer to £1.2 million rather than the £2.4 million estimated by Rochdale Council. His defence lawyer, Richard Orme, argued that Malik had purchased a "job lot" of counterfeit stock for £6,000, intending to sell it for around £20,000. However, Judge Jason Macadam stated that the £2.4 million figure represented the potential losses to the legitimate brands had customers purchased the counterfeit items instead.

The court's findings highlight the significant impact of counterfeit goods on legitimate businesses, with the judge emphasising the importance of protecting brand integrity. Malik's case serves as a reminder of the legal consequences associated with the sale of counterfeit merchandise.

As the case progresses, further sentencing details will be determined by the court, and Malik faces potential penalties for his actions. This incident underscores the ongoing issue of counterfeit goods in the retail market, which continues to affect both consumers and legitimate businesses alike.

articles.title: Are there really fairies in Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: The Fairies’ Chapel is part geology and part story — a riverside niche that inspired Victorian storytellers and still sparks local legend, but the stones speak a different language to the folklore.
articles.summary: The Fairies’ Chapel is part geology and part story — a riverside niche that inspired Victorian storytellers and still sparks local legend, but the stones speak a different language to the folklore.
articles.body:
Walk the Spodden through Healey Dell and you’ll come to a narrow cleft the locals call the Thrutch, where the water has hollowed a church‑like niche in the rock. The name “Fairies’ Chapel” belongs to that place: it’s a charming local toponym and a focus for the Dell’s long tradition of storytelling — but the site itself is a recognised nature reserve with a heritage centre, visitor facilities and an industrial‑archaeological story that you can confirm on the borough’s website. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

The Dell’s human record is plain: the valley hosts mill ruins, lodges, a recreated heritage centre and a former Lancashire & Yorkshire Railway viaduct now recorded on the National Heritage List for England (Healey Dell Viaduct, Grade II). Those are facts you can check in official listings and conservation records; the viaduct’s listed status is part of the site’s documented history rather than its fairy lore. ([historicengland.org.uk](https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1317784?utm_source=openai))

The fairies arrive in the written record through collectors of local tradition. The best‑known literary source is John Roby’s Traditions of Lancashire (first published 1829), which prints a full romance of the Fairies’ Chapel: a miller, a Lady Eleanor, a Fairy Queen and prophecies tied to a grotto beyond the waterfall. Roby’s work is an important record of regional storytelling, but it is a collection of folklore and narrative rather than an archival record of events. In other words, Roby preserves what people told one another; he does not provide independent proof that supernatural beings lived in the Dell. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm?utm_source=openai))

Local interpretive material — including the Healey Dell Heritage Centre — explains how geology and water action could produce the “pulpit, reading desk and seats” that earlier visitors described, and it records that part of the feature described as the chapel was lost in a great flood in the 1830s. The precise year reported varies between accounts: the heritage guide names a flood on 4 July 1838, while other long‑running guides give 1839 as the date. That discrepancy shows how oral and popular histories can diverge from contemporary documentary records; I could not find a single primary archive entry here that settles which year is definitively correct. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/history/?utm_source=openai))

So: are there really fairies in Healey Dell? If you mean literal supernatural beings, there is no verifiable documentary evidence to support their existence — references are folklore, literary retelling and local tradition rather than legal records, surveys or conservation reports. If you mean has the place inspired and preserved stories of fairies, witches and a Fairy King, the answer is an emphatic yes: those tales have been collected, retold and used to interpret the landscape for well over a century, and they form an important part of local cultural heritage. ([gutenberg.org](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/25256/25256-h/25256-h.htm?utm_source=openai))

Visitors today can enjoy both layers: the real, recorded features of the Dell (wildlife, waterfalls, mill remains and a listed viaduct) and the imaginative pleasures of a place that has gathered romance and regional folklore. Treat the Fairies’ Chapel as you would any good local story — a memorable part of Healey’s identity that sits alongside verifiable history, not in its place.

Rochdale AFC's Youth Team faced a disappointing end to their U17 PDL Cup group match on 15 September 2026, drawing 2-2 after leading for most of the game. This match marked the team's second game in the tournament.

The Youth Team initially took the lead with two goals, showcasing strong performance throughout the match. However, they were pegged back late on, allowing their opponents to equalise in the final minutes.

This result means that the Youth Team will need to secure a win in their upcoming matches to improve their chances of advancing in the tournament. The next fixture is crucial for their progression in the U17 PDL Cup.

Fans and supporters of Rochdale AFC will be keen to see how the Youth Team responds in their next game, as they aim to bounce back from this setback.

articles.title: Littleborough and Wardle Brass Bands Prepare for National Finals on 20 September
articles.excerpt: Littleborough Brass Band and Wardle Community Band showcased their test pieces at a concert in Dearnley ahead of the National Brass Band Championships of Great Britain at York Barbican.
articles.content_html:
Littleborough Brass Band and Wardle Community Band are gearing up for the National Brass Band Championships of Great Britain, taking place on Sunday, 20 September, at York Barbican. Both bands performed their test pieces during a concert held at St Andrew’s Church in Dearnley, Littleborough, on Sunday, 13 September.

Littleborough Brass Band, under the direction of conductor Max Stannard, played 'Snow Island' by Thierry Deleruyelle, competing in the Third Section. Meanwhile, Wardle Community Band, led by conductor Jane Conway, performed 'Heroes of the North' by Peter Graham, preparing for the Fourth Section contest.

Matthew Ryan, a brass band adjudicator and conductor, attended the concert to provide feedback to both bands on their performances. Jonathan Coomer, secretary of Littleborough Brass Band, emphasised the importance of performing in front of an audience as part of their preparation for the finals.

The concert attracted a full audience at St Andrew’s Church, showcasing the talent and dedication of both bands as they make their final preparations for the national competition this week.
